doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Big-band audiences then and music today
summary: Marty contrasts young audiences for melodic big-band music with rap; Monk offers a theory about rhythm.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Can you put this in perspective for me a little bit? The music that you were playing at that time, what was the average age of the audience that would come to see you?

The audience? I’d say anywhere from 18 to 25, 30, somewhere around there. They were young kids. You know this is something that you mention, funny you mention that because I keep thinking about the fact that the music that we loved then, excuse me, with the big band, it was like jazz tinged. Everything was jazz flavored. Nowadays they’ve got these 18 year old kids, listening to rap or whatever other stuff they’re listening to, and I say what happened to these kids, when we were 18, that when they heard the Glenn Miller band or a Charlie Barnet or a Count Basie or a Duke Ellington, they went crazy. Don’t these kids have the same kind of feeling that we did in those days?
That was the popular music of the day, what you were playing.

But that’s beside the point. The point is even today, you listen to a Glenn Miller arrangement, and the music is so melodic and so beautiful. I mean I remember even when Buddy DeFranco was fronting the Glenn Miller band a friend of mine called me and he says, “Marty, would you like to go see the Glenn Miller band?” I says, “where? He’s dead.” He said, “no, but Buddy DeFranco’s got the band, they’re going to be at St. Regis Roof.” I said, “I’d love to.” He says, “you’re my guest.” And we went up there and I

swear to you the band, I mean the kids in the band were like 18, 19 years old, young kids because he couldn’t afford to get older guys. When the band started to play the theme I had a lump in my throat and I got tears in my eyes. Because I said, “I don’t care how you feel about the band, the music was so beautiful and so romantic and so melodic. And I don’t understand these kids today. Don’t they hear a melody? I mean can’t they hear something when it makes sense?
Well I have a small theory about that.

And I think that the parts of the music that get the emphasis has changed a lot. And you mentioned there, the melodic end of it. That’s what you heard, but as soon as you heard that theme song you heard the melodic end of it. But I think starting in the 50s and so forth it switched to the rhythmic end of it a lot more. And when you say rap, that’s almost total rhythm. It’s almost total rhythm.
Well to their ears it’s music but it’s almost totally rhythmic and also even the way they make the records now, the rhythm is so much out there, farther than any melody that might even be there.

Well maybe I’m prejudiced, I can’t fathom listening to something when it doesn’t have melodic lines, they’re just talking it. I mean that’s like Phil Harris talking “Sixteen Tons.” Remember that song? “Sixteen Tons.” Or Rex Harrison doing “My Fair Lady.” I mean he did a great job, but he wasn’t singing a song. I want to hear — Bobby Darin, you know, who is my favorite singer.
